Among 163,681 participants (mean age 53.7 ± 14.4 years; 35.6% female), 10,445 (6.4%) initiated GLP-1RAs. At 1-year follow-up, Treatment cohort had lower likelihood of all-cause (aOR=0.28, 95%CI: 0.28,0.29) and alcohol-related (aOR=0.20; 95%CI: 0.20,0.21) hospitalizations, death (aOR=0.20, 95%CI: 0.19,0.21), and MCVE (aOR=0.72, 95%CI: 0.71,0.74). Exploratory analyses showed that these associations remained consistent at 3 and 5 years. GLP-1RA initiation was associated with reduced risk of MCVE, hospitalization, and mortality among adults with AUD and overweight/obesity, supporting potential role of GLP-RAs in AUD. Prospective studies are warranted.

title: SCIMP mediated innate and adaptive immunomodulation after subarachnoid hemorrhage.
journal: Neurotherapeutics : the journal of the American Society for Experimental NeuroTherapeutics
abstract: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) induces robust neuroinflammation, characterized by rapid activation of innate immune cells and subsequent engagement of adaptive immunity. The transmembrane adaptor protein SLP adaptor and C-terminal Src kinase-interacting membrane protein (SCIMP) has emerged as a critical regulator of immune signaling in microglia and antigen-presenting cells. SCIMP interacts with Toll-like receptors (TLRs) and recruits Lyn kinase, forming the SCIMP-TLR-Lyn signaling axis that fine-tunes downstream inflammatory cascades. Activation of this axis modulates cytokine production, balancing pro and anti-inflammatory responses, and influences antigen presentation to T cells, thereby shaping adaptive immune activation. Experimental models of SAH demonstrate that SCIMP deficiency exacerbates neuroinflammation, disrupts the blood-brain barrier, and worsens neurological outcomes, whereas SCIMP activation attenuates inflammatory injury and promotes tissue recovery. These findings highlight the SCIMP-TLR-Lyn pathway as a pivotal mediator of both innate and adaptive immunomodulation after SAH and suggest its potential as a therapeutic target for mitigating secondary brain injury.

title: From evidence to practice: Expert consensus for sleep dysfunction in Parkinson disease.
abstract: Our Parkinson disease sleep recommendations provide an evidence-informed, expert consensus framework rather than a rigid treatment hierarchy. Emphasizing individualized risk-benefit assessment and practical point-of-care guidance, we address therapeutic decisions where definitive evidence is lacking while strongly supporting rigorous prospective trials to advance care.

title: Fertility-Related Distress in Young Adult Survivors of Childhood Cancer: Prevalence and Key Predictors.
abstract: Impaired fertility can occur as a late effect of childhood cancer treatment. This study aimed to assess the prevalence and predictors of fertility-related distress in young adult childhood cancer survivors, compared to a general population sample. This nationwide, population-based cross-sectional study included 1333 women (67% response rate) and 1213 men (54%) aged 19-40, who had been treated for cancer in Sweden between ages 0 and 17. Eligible survivors were identified through the National Quality Registry for Childhood Cancer in Sweden. A comparison group was randomly selected from the Swedish Population Registry, comprising 493 (51% response rate) women and 326 (34%) men. The study combined clinical registry data and self-report measures. The main outcome was high fertility-related distress assessed with the six-dimension Reproductive Concerns After Cancer (RCAC) scale, with high distress defined as a mean score above 4. The comparison group completed only the three RCAC dimensions relevant to adults without a history of cancer. Group comparisons were undertaken using logistic regression, with analyses stratified by sex. A total of 44% of female and 23% of male survivors reported high fertility-related distress in at least one RCAC dimension. Distress was most prevalent in the Fertility potential dimension, and both female and male survivors were significantly more likely to report high distress regarding fertility potential than women and men in the comparison group. Among survivors, high fertility-related distress across several RCAC dimensions was associated with not having children, the desire for (additional) children, having undergone intensive cancer treatments or fertility-preservation procedures, receiving ongoing hormone replacement therapy, and experiencing concurrent anxiety and depressive symptoms. The results underscore the need to address fertility-related concerns in the follow-up care of childhood cancer survivors.

title: Macrophage Extracellular Vesicle-Camouflaged Framework Nucleic Acid Nanospheres Reprogram Lactate Metabolism-Immune Feedback Loops for Synergistic Chemoimmunotherapy of Glioblastoma.
abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) and blood-brain tumor barrier (BBTB) severely limited drug delivery into the brain, while aberrant aerobic glycolysis in the tumor microenvironment caused excessive lactate accumulation and drove immunosuppression. These factors together constituted the core obstacles to glioblastoma (GBM) therapy. From the perspective of metabolism-immune crosstalk, we engineered a brain‑targeted nucleic acid nanosphere (TE@siP‑DNS/DOX) featuring high BBB/BBTB penetrability, which orchestrated a "triple‑linked" strategy integrating glycolysis blockade, immune microenvironment remodeling, and synergistic therapeutic potentiation. The nanosphere was constructed with a self‑assembled core of PKM2‑targeting siRNA and framework nucleic acids loaded with doxorubicin (DOX), shielded by a biomimetic shell of T7 peptide‑modified macrophage extracellular vesicles. Leveraging transcytosis and T7‑mediated active targeting, TE@siP‑DNS/DOX efficiently traversed the barriers and preferentially accumulated at tumor sites. DOX simultaneously provoked chemotherapy and immunogenic cell death, igniting robust CD8⁺ T cell‑mediated antitumor immunity, whereas siRNA‑mediated PKM2 silencing curtailed glycolysis, lessened lactate production, rewired metabolic circuitry, and forced macrophage polarization toward the M1 antitumor phenotype, thereby dismantling the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (iTME). Transcriptomic analysis further confirmed that metabolic and immune-related pathways were significantly enriched following TE@siP-DNS/DOX treatment, providing transcriptional evidence for its dual modulation of the metabolic-immune feedback loop. In vivo studies substantiated that TE@siP‑DNS/DOX markedly inhibited tumor growth and prolonged survival in orthotopic GBM-bearing mice. Collectively, this nanoplatform, through a synergistic feedback loop integrating metabolic regulation and immune activation, provides a good therapeutic strategy and research paradigm for enhanced glioma therapy. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Glioblastoma therapy is impeded by a multifaceted barrier system encompassing the blood-brain barrier, metabolic dysregulation, lactate accumulation, and immunosuppression. Here, we engineered a brain-targeted nucleic acid nanosphere that integrates glycolysis blockade, immune remodeling, and chemotherapeutic sensitization via a single platform. By combining PKM2 silencing with doxorubicin-loaded framework nucleic acids and T7-modified macrophage vesicles, the nanosphere achieves efficient barrier penetration, lactate reduction, M1 macrophage repolarization, and immunogenic cell death. This metabolism-immune feedback loop synergistically suppresses orthotopic tumors and extends survival. Our study provides a paradigm for treating brain tumors through concurrent metabolic reprogramming and antitumor immunity, offering a translatable strategy for overcoming therapy resistance in glioblastoma.

title: A hypothesis framework linking the menopausal transition, sleep and brain waste clearance: Insights from experimental models.
abstract: The menopausal transition is increasingly recognized as a neuroendocrine transition with implications for brain health, sleep, cognition and vulnerability to neurodegenerative disease. Fluctuating and declining ovarian hormones coincide with sleep disruption, vasomotor symptoms, cognitive complaints, neuroinflammation and altered blood-brain barrier integrity. Current preclinical models each capture selected components of the menopause transition and provide essential mechanistic insights into the effect of ovarian hormone loss on the brain. Across these models, endocrine change is associated with impairments in hippocampal and prefrontal-dependent cognition, altered sleep-wake regulation, vascular dysfunction, glial activation, disrupted synaptic and mitochondrial homeostasis and exacerbation of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease-like pathology. An emerging but understudied mechanism linking menopause, sleep and neurodegeneration is the glymphatic system, a sleep-dependent brain waste clearance pathway. This review synthesises current evidence to highlight how menopause-related sleep disruption, vascular dysfunction, neuroinflammation and potential alterations in brain-waste clearance may converge to shape cognitive ageing and neurodegenerative disease risk.

title: Acoustic stimuli-enhanced environmental enrichment remodulates cortical processing of sound azimuth in adult female rats.
abstract: Acoustic stimuli-enhanced environmental enrichment (AEE) has been shown to significantly facilitate the behavioral and neuronal processing of sound by promoting plasticity in the auditory system. However, the mechanisms through which acoustic stimulation contributes to enrichment-induced effects remain largely unexplored. Here we found that AEE exposure during adulthood significantly improved the sound-azimuth discrimination abilities of female rats compared to age-matched naïve controls. Furthermore, AEE enhanced the sound-azimuth selectivity of neurons in the primary auditory cortex. These changes in the behavioral and cortical processing of sound azimuth were accompanied by an increase in the density of cortical parvalbumin-labeled (PV+) inhibitory interneurons. Interestingly, the rats reared in an identical enriched condition but without extra sound exposure also exhibited sharper cortical azimuth tuning and more cortical PV+ interneurons compared to the naïve rats. However, the post-rearing effects in these rats were less pronounced than those observed in the AEE rats, indicating an additional contribution of acoustic stimulation to enrichment-induced changes in the mature auditory cortex. Together, these findings provide compelling evidence for the significant influence of AEE on behavioral and cortical processing of sound azimuth. They suggest that AEE is an effective paradigm for promoting experience-dependent plasticity in the auditory system, even beyond the traditionally recognized critical period.

title: Baseline suicidal thoughts are associated with ECT non-remission and cognitive side effects: A network outcome analysis.
abstract: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is effective for severe depression, yet remission is not universal and cognitive side effects remain a concern. Individual depressive symptoms may provide prognostic information beyond overall severity scores. In a multicentre cohort from the Dutch ECT Consortium, we applied network outcome analysis to seven symptoms harmonized across the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale and Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS). Outcomes were remission (N = 792) and in exploratory analysis, cognitive side effects (N = 100). Robustness was assessed through bootstrapping and sensitivity analyses, including established clinical predictors, an alternative remission definition, and multivariable logistic regression. Suicidal thoughts were associated with lower odds of remission (OR 0.77, bootstrapped confidence interval [bCI] 0.68-0.84) and higher odds of cognitive side effects (OR 1.34, bCI 1.15-2.02), with 98-100% and 72-91% bootstrap edge presence across sensitivity analyses, respectively. Reduced appetite was associated with higher remission odds (OR 1.08, bCI 1.03-1.22), with 70-94% bootstrap edge presence across sensitivity analyses, but the association was absent in the MADRS-specific analysis. Tension/anxiety was associated with higher odds of cognitive side effects (OR 1.26, bCI 1.14-1.92), with 77-84% bootstrap edge presence. After simultaneous covariate adjustment, logistic regression supported associations of suicidal thoughts with both outcomes and tension/anxiety with cognitive side effects; the adjusted cognitive model was exploratory. Baseline symptoms showed distinct associations with ECT outcomes. Suicidal thoughts were associated with both lower remission likelihood and higher odds of cognitive side effects, suggesting potential relevance for clinical monitoring and counselling.

title: Impact of PPAR agonists on seizure suppression to disease modification using status-epilepticus experimental model: Role of the PPAR in metabolic-inflammatory pathway.
abstract: This study explored the potential of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (α/γ) (PPAR modulators) for seizure control and the consequences of status epilepticus (SE) due to their anti-inflammatory and neuro-modulatory properties. A lithium-pilocarpine-induced status epilepticus (SE) model in Wistar rats determined the optimal dose of PPAR modulators (fenofibrate, pemafibrate, and saroglitazar) for seizure suppression. Based on seizure parameters, an efficacy study examined PPAR modulators alone and in combination with ASMs (valproate and perampanel). Evaluations of disease-modifying effects included neurobehavioral tests, electron microscopy for neurodegeneration, immunohistochemistry (NeuN for neuronal viability and GFAP for astrocytosis), Western blotting for PPARα, HMGCS2, NLRP3, and mTOR, and ELISA for antioxidant capacity and neuroinflammatory biomarkers. The optimal doses of fenofibrate, pemafibrate, and saroglitazar were 200, 1.5, and 3 mg/kg, respectively. Compared with the SE-control group, drug-treated groups had higher latency (p<0.001), a lower number and percentage of rats with stage 3-4 seizures (p=0.003, for both), better memory retention (p=0.001), less myelin-sheath/axonal damage (p<0.001), significant differences in protein expressions [NeuN, PPARα, HMGCS2, mTOR, and NLRP3 (p<0.001)], and less neuroinflammation. The PPAR modulators + perampanel group had no stage 3-4 seizures. Compared to valproate alone, fenofibrate+valproate exhibited less neurodegeneration and astrocytosis in the hippocampus and cerebral cortex (p<0.001, for all). All PPAR modulator combinations with ASM groups had significantly higher PPARα and HMGCS2 expression. PPAR modulators fenofibrate, pemafibrate, and saroglitazar have similar seizure-control potential. In the SE model, PPAR modulators with ASM showed significant neuroprotection and increased PPARα expression compared to ASM alone.

title: Choroid plexus volume as a marker of chronotherapeutic responsiveness in major depressive disorder.
abstract: Circadian rhythm disruption is a core feature of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). The choroid plexus (ChP), a circadian-regulated structure involved in cerebrospinal fluid production and immune signalling, has been previously associated with depression and may undergo structural changes in response to chronotherapeutics. The study included 25 patients with MDD and 25 matched healthy controls who underwent MRI. Patients received total sleep deprivation plus light therapy (TSD + LT), consisting of three 36-hour sleep deprivation cycles, each separated by a night of recovery sleep. LT was administered for 30 min every morning. Depressive symptoms, sleep quality, and chronotype were assessed through Beck's Depression Inventory (BDI), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ), respectively. ChP volumes were extracted with FreeSurfer and normalized for intracranial volume. Effects of chronotherapeutics were assessed on BDI, PSQI, and ChP volumes, with treatment response as a between-subject factor. The efficacy of treatment was also investigated stratifying for chronotype. Also, group differences in ChP volume and associations with sleep and BDI scores were explored. TSD + LT reduced depressive symptoms and improved sleep quality, with changes in PSQI associated with symptom improvement. Eveningness predicted greater depressive symptom reduction. At baseline, responders already exhibited larger left ChP volume than controls. Following treatment, a treatment × response interaction emerged for right ChP volume, showing a significant reduction in responders. Finally, reductions in both right and left ChP volumes predicted clinical improvement, and sleep quality improvement predicted right ChP volume reduction. This is the first study showing that chronotherapy modulates ChP structure in MDD, suggesting a link between circadian dysregulation and ChP enlargement proportional to clinical improvement and predicted by sleep amelioration. ChP volume may represent a biomarker of treatment responsiveness and circadian realignment.

title: Brain endothelial interleukin-1 receptor signaling drives the late phase of endotoxin-induced fever.
abstract: Interleukin-1 (IL-1) is a key endogenous pyrogen, yet its cellular targets and temporal role in fever remain incompletely understood. We studied C57BL/6J mice aged 2-6 months using conditional genetic approaches to dissect interleukin-1 receptor type 1 (IL-1R1) signaling in brain endothelial cells, neural lineages, and TRPV1-expressing sensory neurons. Fever was induced by intravenous administration of lipopolysaccharide (LPS; 30 μg/kg), and body temperature was monitored by telemetry. Following LPS administration, mice lacking IL-1R1 in brain endothelial cells exhibited selective attenuation of late-phase fever, whereas the initial febrile phase and the intervening transient hypothermia remained intact. In contrast, deletion of IL-1R1 in neural cells or TRPV1-expressing sensory neurons had no detectable effect on the febrile response. Selective re-expression of IL-1R1 in brain endothelial cells in otherwise receptor-deficient mice restored the late phase of fever, demonstrating that endothelial IL-1R1 signaling is sufficient for this component of the response. Following intraperitoneal administration of IL-1β, mice expressing IL-1R1 selectively in brain endothelial cells maintained an elevated body temperature after the initial handling-induced hyperthermia, whereas the subsequent rapid hypothermic response observed in wild-type mice was not restored. Temporal profiling showed that circulating IL-1β was undetectable during the initial febrile phase, variably elevated thereafter, and consistently elevated during late-phase fever. Together, these findings demonstrate that IL-1 acts in a cell type-specific and temporally restricted manner, with brain endothelial IL-1R1 signaling sustaining the late phase of fever, whereas earlier temperature responses arise through mechanisms independent of endothelial IL-1R1.

title: Persistent neuroimmune alterations in children who are HIV-exposed but uninfected at age 6-7 years: Associations with language development in a South African birth cohort.
abstract: Children who are HIV-exposed but uninfected (HEU) are at increased risk of neurodevelopmental delays, yet neuroimmune pathways linking perinatal HIV exposure to school readiness remain unclear. In the Drakenstein Child Health Study, 267 children (93 HEU, 174 HIV-unexposed [HU]) underwent magnetic resonance spectroscopy in midline parietal grey and left parietal white matter regions at 6-7 years. Peripheral blood serum immune markers were measured in pregnancy and in children at 6 weeks, 2, 3, and 5 years. Linear mixed-effects models characterised child immune trajectories and linear regressions tested associations with creatine-referenced neurometabolite ratios and school readiness scores. Mothers living with HIV had higher sCD14 and lower MMP-9, NGAL, and GM-CSF than mothers without HIV (p < 0.05). Perinatal HIV exposure was associated with altered trajectories of child sCD14, GM-CSF, IL-1β, IL-5, IL-10, and YKL-40. At 6-7 years, children who were HEU had lower parietal grey matter glutamate ratios and lower left parietal white matter choline ratios. By school entry, more frequent associations between child immune markers and neurometabolites were observed, with IL-8 emerging as a recurrent correlate across developmental stages. Children who were HEU had lower language scores than HU peers. Left parietal white matter choline ratios were positively associated with language and overall school readiness in HU children, but not HEU. Perinatal HIV exposure was associated with alterations in immune development, neurometabolites reflecting both white matter maturation and neuronal health, and school readiness. Our findings highlight potential neuroimmune alterations contributing to neurodevelopmental risks in children who are HEU. A single explanatory pathway was not identified, supporting the need for longitudinal studies of neuroimmune, clinical, and environmental contributors to developmental vulnerability in this population.

title: 1H MRS reveals impact of early adversity and age on neurometabolic profiles in women.
abstract: Exposure to early-life stress (ELS), including neglect or abuse, is known for its detrimental effects on brain health. This study investigated how ELS interacts with chronological age to impact on brain metabolism in middle-aged women using proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H MRS) at 3 T. High-quality spectra from the hippocampus (HC) and posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) from 75 women, including 53% with ELS exposure before puberty, were analyzed. Generalized additive models assessed non-linear effects of ELS severity and chronological age on neurometabolites related to neuroinflammation and neurotransmitter cycling. Significant interactions emerged for myo-inositol (Ins) in both regions and glutamine (Gln) in the PCC, where greater ELS severity was linked to age-related increases in Ins and Gln concentrations. These results were robust when additionally controlling for symptoms of depression, anxiety, and PTSD, as well as SES, education, menopause status, and smoking. The observed patterns suggest that ELS exposure before puberty, at the older age range, is associated with glial and glutamatergic alterations that are indicative of neuroinflammation, potentially reflecting vulnerability to adverse brain health outcomes.
